At the universities one studies, they know the way of GOD correctly; that is a "saint-eater" <note>an epithet for one who acts holier-than-thou</note>, he wants to be something special; what the enthusiast <term>Schwermer</term> <gloss>fanatic/enthusiast</gloss> says, there is no need to pay attention to. If GOD wants me pious, He will make me pious when the time comes that I should die; I will still turn then. Why should I make my heart heavy for long? I will be merry as long as I live; I get nothing out of it in the end. I know well what I have, but not what I will get; that I will first experience well then. GOD is gracious and merciful, He will have mercy on me. But hear! What does GOD's word say to this, and our Lord Christ in his Holy Gospel? Whoever wants to follow me, let him take up his cross and follow me: Repent and believe the Gospel: No one can serve two masters: My kingdom is not of this world: Here you have fear, but there your sadness shall be turned into joy, and other such heartfelt sayings more. sample.seedTranslation: that! Was not Cornelius a heathen? Nevertheless, when he fasted and called upon God, God heard him and helped him onto the right path. How much more we Christians, who are baptized into God's most holy name and can surely take comfort and assurance in our baptismal covenant with God. Why do we not strive for it? Whose is the fault? Is it not ours? Why are we so lazy and negligent regarding the eternal, which lasts into all eternity? It is therefore not God's fault, but our own malice, that we will not obey His voice. We spend most of our life with temporal, perishable existence, which in a moment passes away and we with it, God knows how. Even if Weigelius and other such authors use the same kinds of idioms in their writings, what can we and another upright Christian do about that? All sects and heresies make use of the Holy Scripture; should we for that reason also despise, reject, revile, and slander it? Far be it! They may answer for their own affairs, for what they have written. Each one must give an account for himself and be certain of his own actions, teaching, and life, as he would stand before God on that day. We have the Holy Scripture, Moses and the prophets, the Holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ; that is prescribed to us as a rule and guideline for how we should conduct our life. <header>Concluding Speech.</header>
<sig>B iij</sig>
<meta>catchword: The</meta>
This Judge will not look upon a <term>Primarium</term> <gloss>senior church official</gloss> or his entourage, which he draws to himself, nor any king, prince, or lord of the world according to their possessed power, nor their laws, but will judge the life and test it in His fire. Where will your desecrations and revilements, which you have driven against Christ in His members, remain then? It is written: whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness eternally. What, then, do you want to answer for having consciously blasphemed His gift and so wretchedly persecuted the children of Christ? When Christ says, "Whatever you did to these least of my brothers, you did to me," what answer will you then give?

You also despise that I am a layman and have not come from the university with my knowledge, and you spit upon my gift, which I have nevertheless received from GOD as a noble present, which is dearer to me than the whole world. You also desecrate my trade with your spitting and call it, together with my gift, a stench.

How might it go for you when such blasphemies awaken within you in body and soul, and your "fie," with which you spit upon the gift of the Holy Spirit, awakens in you and is ignited by GOD’s wrath, so that the world becomes too narrow for you? What would you then want to give that you had not done such a thing?

I have written of 3 births, as of an eternal, beginningless Divine one, and of a Holy one, in which light and darkness (as GOD's love and wrath) are understood; and of a beginning and temporal one (as of the visible world); and I understand the saltpeter and mercury in the 3rd (birth) as in the created beings.

43. I indicate what is mystery, heavenly, and earthly, as the element and its outflow with 4 elements and the stars. sample.seedTranslation:
<header>Defense Speech. Response.</header>

101. O Mr. Primarius! Where does this stand in my book, that I teach men external ecstasy? Show me that, or it will not be so. I teach them the anointing of JESUS CHRIST, with His tender humanity, of a spiritual nature in us, according to the inward ground of faith, of which Christ says: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him; and he who does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man has no life in him <note>John 6:53-56</note>.

102. For that is the temple of the Holy Spirit, as St. Paul says, where Christ’s flesh and blood remain in us. Item: It is the new rebirth, in which the Holy Spirit researches the depth of the Godhead. It is the poured-out Word of the poured-out divine love, which weds and falls in love with our souls, as the entire New Testament teaches, as it is written, etc.

103. Test whether Christ has taken a form in you. If Christ is to gain a form in us, then that must not be absent. If we are to be branches on the vine of Christ, then we must not cling to another: for no one can serve two hearts, says Christ. Item: My Father will give the Holy Spirit to all who ask Him for it. Item: When that same one shall come, he will glorify you.

# Reſponſio.

### Pasquil.

157. Christ gave the thirsty water of life to drink, but the shoemaker runs every morning to the brandy, or water of death.

### Responsio.

158. Christ offers his children the water of eternal life even today, and gives them to drink of his blood of love; he also gives me that same water to drink for my thirsty soul; for that I thank him eternally, that he has made me alive and seeing through this water; I drink that same water, and that is a water for and against death, about which the Lord Primarius speaks in a perverted way.

159. But that he says I run to brandy every morning, that is not at all true; I neither can nor want to drink brandy, and I have had enmity with brandy for a long time, so that I do not even like to smell it; it is repulsive to me; it surprises me that the Lord Primarius, as a high priest, errs so greatly; it becomes him very badly; if a common man did that, one would say: He is a liar. I hardly know what I should give in answer to such an untruth.

sample.seedTranslation:
Sancyranus lived for no more than five years after Jansenius. An arrogant man, raising himself above all theologians, he so despised the Council of Trent as the work of scholastics and a single Pontiff. What he thought about the doctrine of grace he revealed, being heard to say at one time: "Calvin understood well, but spoke badly." Moreover, being as cautious as possible, he demanded Pythagorean silence from those to whom he spoke ("in secret because of the fear of the Jews," he would say), and he wanted all his letters to be burned. Once, he had imprudently offered poison to a certain priest; he repented immediately, and while the man was proceeding to Poitiers, fearing a denunciation to the local Bishop, he catches up to the man in the middle of his journey and asks to be heard in confession. He then used to tell with a laugh how cunningly he had imposed silence upon a man of dubious faith. A deed worthy of a severe exactor of austere penance! Led by his spirit, the Virgins of Port-Royal deprived themselves of the heavenly bread for many months, even at Easter. The men gave clearer specimens of this penance, some of whom were directors of the Virgins, ascetics, or others who, as penitents, had built their own little huts within the walls of the monastery. For they, not for months but for seven years and more, indeed until the end of their lives, abstained from the table of the Lord as a punishment for their sins.

His first fruit was the *Quaestio Regia* <gloss>Royal Question</gloss>; To what extent is a subject, especially in times of peace, obliged to preserve the life of a prince at the expense of his own life? In it, he reviews more than 30 cases in which he contends that suicide is lawful.

Thus Pascal, I say, not less learnedly and theologically, if you please; unless you prefer to say ironically, by which he mocked his own associates, who did not cease to declaim and write against the Bulls of Innocent and Alexander and other decrees about various nullities. For this writer seemed too fickle to the Jansenists themselves, nay even sometimes of doubtful faith, certainly never fearing to contradict himself if it pleased him, of which he also gave a specimen in the *Provincial Letters*, where he ridicules the doctrine of the Thomist school, which at the beginning he mocks, [but] afterwards commends as his own.

But neither could the power of the King do anything at that time against these men; although he ordered the mandate of accepting the Bull and the same subscription to be entered into the records of the Parliament; and this was an act entirely new and the first of all, by which such a declaration of the King was sent to the Parliament, by which the Pontifical Bull was commanded to be received by royal power as a dogma. The King, therefore, in order to cut off all excuses by which they might exempt themselves from the formula of subscription, requested that a formula be prescribed by the Pontiff himself; that which the Clergy also at the same time begged with highest prayers.

A writer of an intemperate mind and pen, he published very many little works filled with mockery against even the highest dignities and with pestiferous doctrines. Quesnel also praised Gerberon, criticizing nothing in his letters to Boileau, a friend of the Prelate, except that the book was published too quickly and at an inopportune time, namely, when Noailles was called to the Purple <note>the rank of Cardinal</note> by Innocent XII at the request of the King.

Shortly after the *Problem* followed the *Case of Conscience*. The question was asked: whether a confessor has well absolved a cleric who confesses that he does not submit in his mind to the judgment of the Church concerning the text of the Authors, yet displays external submission and reverence to it in silence? The response, subscribed by 40 Theologian Doctors, [was] that this opinion of the Cleric is neither new, nor singular, nor condemned by the Church: [and] that such a person is neither to be urged further, nor held to be suspect. Cardinal Noailles condemned this response as well, and at the same time took care that nothing sinister or injurious be published against the subscribed Doctors, who also all later, except for two, excused the deed.

But these threats soon vanished. Since neither the acts of the Parliament nor the error of the abbot seemed of such importance that they could stir a prudent suspicion that acceptance would be denied, and the Dauphin had even given in writing a public testimony of the Catholic faith and his firm adherence to it, after two years of exhaustion finally spent on examinations and the collation of texts, the famous Bull *Unigenitus* <gloss>Only-Begotten</gloss> was signed by Clement XI on September 8, 1713, after everything had first been examined and the points revised by Trémoille, and it was published two days later, on September 10. In it, one hundred and one propositions excerpted from the work of Quesnel are condemned "in the lump," as they say, namely, as false, impious, heretical, etc., with these and other censures added to be applied respectively to each. It is added that many other similar and related propositions are contained therein that are worthy of condemnation, and that the text of the scripture itself is corrupted by the disapproved Montenfus edition. Wherefore the whole book, published or to be published in any language, is prohibited and condemned.

The Pope replied that he would be content if the Opponents accepted the Bull in relation to the instruction of those 40 Bishops; but it was not this, but another, namely with various restrictions and distinctions of senses, that Cavalier demanded. At last, having laid aside all shame, various demands of the Pope were exposed by the opponents through Trémoille, and among these a national Council, from which, so that an appeal to a General one could be made, they dared to establish as a foundation. § 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

The thunders of the Vatican were now being prepared; Noailles was judged by the College of Cardinals itself to be unworthy of the purple. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having completed a certain scheme of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by those accepting, they offered them a writing of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle column of which were the propositions of Quesnell themselves, on one side the obvious sense, on the other some other Catholic one, or at least one capable of excuse.

And with these, all the Duke’s plans conceived in his mind for bringing the Cardinal back to the path were finally overturned.

Meanwhile the Appellants triumphed, though not without grief for the death of Quesnel, their leader most esteemed after Arnauld, from whom all this present cause was derived. It is not pleasing here to weave the history of this man’s life; it is helpful to add only two things worthy of memory to what has already been said about him. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain Priest, who, having at last wiped away the darkness of errors, was returned to himself and the Church, and produced it. These were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his own were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum was almost this: Union and concord: faith in the secret: circumspection in speech according to the varying condition of men: ambiguity <note>original: "amphibologia"</note> in various heads of Religion: he wished it to be said that they use Christ present in the Eucharist, not only by faith or figure, as the heterodox do, but neither by transubstantiation or substantially or really, as Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible manner. In the Sacrament of penance, they were to urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. That they should openly impugn sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, and at other times through the vagueness of words, so that a way out might be open to the pressed: that they should uniquely extol victorious grace: and thus many other things. The Cardinal, before he would accept the bull, requested that it be examined. Upon these being rejected, he proposed a formula to be signed, by which he would not only accept the bull simply, but also retract all that he had written wrongly in his pastoral Instruction. At the same time, having convened a particular council in the Lateran Basilica, he declared the constitution *Unigenitus* <note>original: "Unigenitus" - a papal bull issued by Pope Clement XI in 1713, condemning the errors of Pasquier Quesnel</note> as a Rule of faith. Since Noailles was still prevaricating, he broke off all further communication with him. King Louis XV also suppressed by decree those same twelve articles which shameless peddlers of nonsense had published as if submitted by the Pope himself for the explanation of the bull.

Driven so often and so strongly, the Cardinal finally seemed to waver; he was certainly deliberating about promulgating the Bull. The letter of his thirty parish priests caused a delay, who, after it had been suppressed and torn up by the King's order, openly declared by means of flying papers and voices that they would be under the authority of one God and an ecumenical council. Added to this were the examples and exhortations of his three principal episcopal colleagues of Sens, Montpellier, and Auxerre, under whose name and approval, and under whose auspices, whole reams of mandates, instructions, letters, professions of faith, notes, and other papers filled with errors and calumnies were produced. Noailles did not, in fact, approve of this much anymore: yet he was held back; he hesitated, although he saw greater scandals and detriments to the Church always growing gradually. *There is one merely spiritual manducation of the flesh of Christ, about which John chapter 6 treats; another is sacramental, which is instituted in the Supper of the Lord. Therefore the very flesh of Christ in the sacramental [manducation] is In, Under, and With that Bread, and that Wine in a manner of corporal presence: and is taken together with the sign itself by anyone approaching the Supper, even with an impure mouth.* Answer. As if, although sacramental manducation has signs for the sake of teaching and relieving our infirmity, which a merely spiritual manducation does not have; yet the very thing of the Sacrament, namely the flesh of Christ (which is one and the same in both, that is, in spiritual and in Sacramental manducation) is eaten in a different manner, and with a different mouth, in this sacramental one than in that merely spiritual one. And that manner, or the mouth suitable for eating the flesh of Christ itself, is faith. What then? Osiander is deceived, and indeed childishly, who thinks that the flesh of Christ itself is different, or is eaten differently, in spiritual manducation than in sacramental. But if the flesh of Christ is the same, then it is received with the same mouth, with the same teeth, with the same stomach: namely, spiritually, not corporally: by faith, not by the mouth: by the spirit, not by the belly. And these, dearest brothers, are all the minutest arguments of this monitor who is enticing you toward a new doctrine; how inept, absurd, <term>asyllogista</term> <gloss>illogical</gloss>, and even blasphemous they are, you yourselves can easily see, as I hope you already do. For a word is sufficient to the wise, as the old proverb says. Although there were enough ineptitudes and errors in what Osiander has written up to this point, for a conclusion he wanted to add others no less significant, so that, compelled by the force of truth and imprudently, he might reveal to you the foulness, not to say impiety, of that doctrine which he yet exhorts you to embrace. That doctrine which he adds, and which follows entirely from the oral manducation <note>the theory that the body of Christ is eaten physically by the mouth</note>, is that even the unworthy—not the Turks, not the Jews, not the Pagans as he calls them (for they would neither approach the supper nor be admitted if known)—but those who externally profess the name of Christ, yet inside are mockers of God, impious and faithless men approaching the supper, he wants, with his impious and impure mouth, to partake of the most sacred body of Christ itself. What more horrible thing can be said? But when the Pelagians brought the baptism of infants (whom they impiously contended were free from Original sin) into contempt, the Fathers took the opposite path, and above all the African Church, as was proper, extolled baptism in amazing ways and demonstrated that its power was immense: finally, however, they also wanted it to be absolutely necessary for salvation. In which, certainly (let it be said with the peace of such great men), no one (who will acquiesce to the word of God, even with Osiander himself as a witness here) can deny that they erred. Whence this error was also obliquely censured in the 4th Council of Carthage, chapter 100, and it was expressly forbidden that women should baptize. But with all kinds of errors later flourishing in the Church of God, at the Council of Florence around the year of the Lord 1439, it was constituted by Eugenius IV what Osiander says here, so that in a case of necessity, first a layman, afterwards if no layman were present, a woman could baptize an infant. You see, therefore, brothers, what supporters Osiander has for this opinion of his: namely, Papist men, deciding all things according to the whim of their own minds in the most corrupt times of the Church, not from the word of God.

To conclude this point, although the works and judgments of God are hidden and unknown to us, they are nevertheless always most just. Nor does it follow that if He is occupied in the same work as we humans, He nonetheless operates viciously, as we do. But because you are very often and very rightly instructed about these matters by your Pastors, and because the scope of this entire disputation is solely to demonstrate that the teaching of this monitor <note>referring to Lucas Osiander</note> is both false and by no means full or sincere, I do not think it necessary to add more on this subject, even though it is a far weightiest argument.

->CONCERNING IDOLS.<-

It remains, therefore, that we also briefly discuss the chapter he added last. It concerns idols. This was not mentioned by Osiander so much out of any necessity of time or of idolatry (which, by the grace of God the Best and Greatest, remains absent among you), but rather to publicly defame all of you, however untimely the occasion he seized upon, and to bring you into hatred and ill will before all Magistrates. For what other purpose does that tail <note>a metaphorical reference to the final section of Osiander’s work</note> of yours have, Osiander, other than for you to vomit forth your poison against us under that honeyed speech and that <term>θεοφρονήσει</term> <gloss>reverent thoughtfulness/divine wisdom</gloss> most exquisitely written by the correction of all your colleagues, and for you to wish for us to be held guilty? Therefore, in that entire writing of yours, the voice indeed was the voice of Jacob, but the hands were the hands of Esau <note>a reference to Genesis 27:22; meaning the words seemed pious, but the intent was hostile</note>, that is, yours. Therefore, you accuse us verbosely because in these civil wars of ours, certain idols were <unclear>in some places by our people</unclear> <column-break/>

THE LAST NUMBER IS CONCLUDED
Observation XIX follows.

OBSERVATION XIX. ON LOCAL VISITATION.

*On the Visitation of Ecclesiastical Persons.*

Firstly, let every parish priest and beneficiary be interrogated regarding his name, surname, parents, and birthplace. Then, let the letters of investiture and admission to the cure be requested from him, if he holds a beneficed cure.
Thirdly, let him be interrogated how often he confesses in a year and to whom.
Fourthly, let his books be seen: whether, besides others, he has a Breviary of Constance with a Directory, the Roman Catechism, the Council of Trent, and the Synodal Statutes of this Diocese: also a book on cases of conscience, and indeed some approved postils <note>Collections of sermons or commentaries on scriptures</note>, as they are called, with Bibles, and let him read these diligently.
Fifthly, let the Visitors sometimes make an experiment with the simpler and suspicious ones by interrogating them regarding various things pertaining to the canonical hours, the ceremonies of the Church, and the administration of the sacraments, whether they are practiced in them or not.

Whether any celebrate sacrifice outside a sacred place, on a portable altar, without the license of the Ordinary.

sample.seedTranslation: and those who are ill for a long time also die with tranquility. From that, I elicit that from a tranquil or heavy resolution, the soul cannot be elicited from the body in a good or bad state after this life, as some ignorant people argue, because death follows the disposition of nature by the law of all. But it is by divine dispensation. Sometimes the saints die much more painfully than the reprobate, and sometimes conversely. For we read that Augustine, Martin, and Bernard departed in heavy pains. And we also read of others who died in such tranquility that their bodies could not even be buried, as Gregory narrates of a certain count who was found to be as holy as he had been believed to be, long after he had rested in the tomb, from the fragrance of his body and the integrity of his body. In the Lives of the Fathers, we also read of two married people, a holy man and a vicious wife, whose husband died with great lack of tranquility and pain, but the woman died with great tranquility and peace. And afterward, it was revealed that the husband was blessed, but the wife was damned. For God purges the elect in the present so that they may be secure afterward. Conversely, he remunerates the reprobate here for their good deeds so that they have nothing to hope for regarding their reward in the future, as is evident in Luke 16 concerning the rich glutton and the holy Lazarus. We believe, however, that the blessed mother of the Lord, Mary, migrated from this age without pain, just as she gave birth to the Savior of the ages without pain. And similarly, John, to whom the Virgin was entrusted at the cross. And we find very many elect of God preserved from the pains of death by a special privilege. Therefore, he who hopes to possess a peaceful resolution of his body should study to preserve his life in innocence, for a bad death, even if it is painful, does not follow a good life. But who leads the souls out as they depart from the body, since they are no longer in their own power? It is necessary, therefore, that they be led by others. To this, although we do not find a certain answer in the scriptures, we can estimate that the angels to whom they are committed lead them out, or if they are to be damned, also.

tempting him whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not. "Show me," he said, "the coin of the tribute." And they offered him a denarius having in itself the image of Caesar and the superscription with the determined weight. This pertains to our proposition: "Whose is this image and superscription?" Certainly Caesar's. It is to be observed, therefore, first whether that appearing spirit has the image of Christ, who is the truth, by His own testimony: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." Which truth excludes all falsity, vanity, and lying. If, therefore, it is found in this spirit that it mingles no falsity, vanity of boastful praise, and arrogance in its manifestation, it is to be presumed to be of a good spirit. If, however, in the opposite mode, it is to be held as suspect, just as in the temptation of Christ, Matthew 4: it suggested gluttony, vain glory, and avarice. And in the temptation of the first woman, it suggested the desire of loftiness, saying: "You shall be as God." And it swore, saying: "For God knows." For that spirit is a liar and the father of lies, nor did it stand in the truth, but is deceitful and fraudulent, and such things proceed from its heart even if it speaks the truth, as is evident in the Gospel, where it is ordered by Christ to be silent even about the truth, because it covers its deceitfulness under it.

<margin>Fourth Mode</margin>
The fourth mode of discerning is if there is the superscription on the denarius, that is, apostolic doctrine and a teacher approved by the church, so that nothing be in the responses of that spirit or in its gestures that derogates from the faith, or from good morals and the rites of the church according to canon laws or conciliar decrees, or against the institutions of the Holy Roman Church. And this is against heretics, deceivers, sorcerers, diviners, and enchanters. The vessel of election, Paul, certifies us to the Galatians 1: "But though we or an angel from heaven preach a gospel to you besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema." Another is the key of excellence which Christ has as man, and such he could communicate to ministers or priests, who are "dispensers of the mysteries of God." And the priests use that key not lost by Christ in the administration of the sacraments of the new testament. And thus the truth is saved in both, that is, God alone forgives sins by the key of authority, priests by the key of ministry. This is the summary of the blessed Thomas, Part III, q. 54, art. 1 and 4. With which Thomas of Argentina agrees in the fourth book, dist. 18. And he puts the example of a prince who has the principal authority of opening and closing a castle or city; through this, however, he does not exclude the porter to whom he has entrusted the keys. He puts another example: an Emperor gives his officials the power to punish evildoers; if, however, they seek pardon and he does this or that, he releases them free; there the officials have the power of the ministry, the prince the power of excellence. So it is concerning Christ and the priests. Christ has the key of excellence in that he uses this key immediately by the merit of his most sacred passion, by this not excluding the ministry of the priests; therefore he said: "Whatever you bind upon earth will be bound also in heaven." Therefore, in confession, much guilt is forgiven and also penalty. And if it is objected that all guilt is forgiven in contrition, therefore the priest does not forgive any. It is answered that there is no true and sufficient contrition without a firm purpose of showing, from the definition of contrition, since the precept of God and the tradition of the Church bind one to confession. Likewise, if it is said that venial sins are forgiven by the sprinkling of blessed water, and by general confession, etc., it is answered according to Saint Thomas, this is as to guilt by reason of the annexed contrition, not as to the whole penalty. I promise you that I will do all of that. ¶ That, however, you will look to by your prudence, by what reason you provide well for your fortunes and my name. Farewell.

<note>Large decorative drop cap 'A' in red and brown ink, featuring a central circular geometric motif surrounded by foliate patterns.</note>
An arduous cause impelled me to write to you at this time. For when I heard that you were occupied with the greatest matters, I would have deferred my business to another time, had it not been of such a nature that, if neglected by me, it could not be corrected by the counsel or aid of any other man afterward. You will bear with me, therefore, if I have interrupted you when you are agitating the greatest matters. I think you remember what words Tiro used when we both met him on the day before the Kalends of March. For when he affirmed that he was returning to grace with me with a good mind, and said that no remnants of hatred remained in him, you ordered me not only to be of an equitable mind but also to be confident and not to suspect anything further about you. I, however, by holding great faith in his words and your authority, had put away and deferred from my mind every memory of the injuries and insults that had been between us. What followed from that, you will hear better from this man whom I send to you, to whom I gave not only letters but also commands which he might bring to you concerning this matter. For after you departed from us, things (as you thought) being composed between me and him, Saturninus arrived, who (as you know) is the most seditious of all; he disturbed everything and stirred up such hatred that my fortune has never been in a worse place. For (as it is wont to be said of a disease) that evil recrudesces sometimes more harshly than it began, which can be cured by no other doctor than by you yourself. Wherefore, if you wish me to be safe, if you wish my fortunes to be whole, take care that you fly to us; there is need of speed, lest I be directed to where at no time—I do not say I may be able to be helped—but not even salvation itself, if it wished, could extract me. Farewell.

in the accusations which were being thrown against you, that he rendered all the judges most favorable to you and hostile to your accusers. Everyone praised the talent of this orator. They approved of your case, and they lauded the equity of the judges. When, however, it came to the sentencing, the applause of everyone was such that they did not rejoice less in the matter than if the common business were being handled. I wished to write these things to you so that I might lighten your mind of that solicitude by which (as I know) you were much afflicted. Farewell.

<note>A large, decorative red initial 'H' marks the beginning of this section.</note> I give thanks to you, and great ones indeed, that you have freed me from the greatest solicitude and annoyance. But with no less pleasure did it affect me that you wrote to me about my patron, a most modest and eloquent man. For I am delighted greatly by his praise and his most magnificent duty. For even if I had never doubted about my case, which could not have been given against me in a lawsuit, yet because in judgments, no differently than in navigating, a danger often threatens, and the one who is the pilot is skilled in his art, I was always fearing lest the equity of the case, or some other fortune, might not have had that which I desired. I rejoice, therefore, that I have drawn such an orator, in whom neither human eloquence nor study was lacking. Soon (as I hope) I will congratulate him myself. Meanwhile, signify to him that I hold great gratitude for his studies and duties. Farewell.

<note>A large, decorative red initial 'V' marks the beginning of this section.</note> You desire that it be signified by me what everyone—both your friends and your fellow citizens—feels about you. There is one opinion: that no one among your equals is greater in talent, but that they fear greatly lest you do not use it sufficiently modestly. Therefore, my Antonius, if good fame delights you, if you sustain the opinion of men which is certainly not small now, see that you do not affect your other virtues, which are great, only with modesty. I understand indeed that you will be a supreme citizen in our city if you know how to use your talent modestly. Which, so that you may do, I ask again and again. Farewell.

sample.seedTranslation:
<note>A decorative red initial 'N' marks the beginning of this paragraph.</note> There is nothing that would be done more willingly than to inform you of the great and most beautiful things that are happening here. For after our city was freed from hostile fear and gave itself to leisure and peace, it is incredible how the state of the Republic began to be reformed and renewed day by day. If there were old discords among our citizens, they were all taken away and lifted. The leaders of the city are entering into new affinities. The fortresses which had been made to yield to the force of wars are being restored with greater care than before and with greater resources, nor were they ever in such value. Very many ancient laws and old statutes which had been neglected are now renewed by our insolence and negligence, and the approval of almost all common offices has been given, by which, if it is obeyed, no one doubts that we may see ourselves somewhat happier in this city (for such is the state of our city) than we have experienced in the long calamity and forced by fortune, which if it had found the same state on which we were relying, and peace, would have been found. I am therefore happy to make all this known to you, so that you who have been most attentive to the hope of our glory may not be ignorant of our happiness at this time. Farewell.

<note>A decorative red initial 'O' marks the beginning of this paragraph.</note> I received great pleasure in my mind from the things you wrote to me. For since I had stood in constant fear, because there was long doubt about your safety, you freed me from great trouble when I learned from your previous letter that your city was freed from the siege that was oppressing it. That letter, however, affected me with such great joy because you announced to me that not only were you exempt from the highest danger, but also the Republic itself is taking on some new form and a happier state day by day. I rejoice, indeed, and more than could be believed, that I am happy for your happiness. I certainly see those excellent foundations of your ancestors' Republic being excited by you with great study. For since the laws in which the safety of your city was placed had come into your forgetfulness, and the ancient custom was not being kept in the city, it was no wonder if your country was led to a siege. But now with laws restored and all good custom repeated, I hope your city will be wider and more opulent.

sample.seedTranslation: <note>A red decorative initial 'E' marks the beginning of the text.</note> I received your letter full of new things. It grieves me that the state of so many magnificent cities and peoples is coming to this. For since in all Latium there is none more illustrious from arms, I see that that ancient glory of Cisalpine Gaul has now almost faded away, reduced to desolation. Oh, fortune has this of the greatest of all things, that when it has reached the summit, then we realize it is at its end. Greece itself (if I may repeat the examples of the ancestors a little further) for a long time not only in disciplines but also in arms conquered Italy; nor was it far from possessing the empire of the orb of lands under the leader Alexander. This having been taken away from human affairs, Greece itself failed. Rome, I want as an example of all the Punic wars and nations, in the name of the empire which it had surpassed from the kings, under the solar empire which it extended to the Parthians, under the emperors, I want not only fame but also its power to have flowed with the boundaries of the world, yet it could not save or protect that empire which had once been donated. Hear this of all its glory, through the change of customs in Greece, it is long since transferred by external kings, sometimes to the West, sometimes to the North. It rejoices in this one thing, and is desolate, that there is no one of those to whom the government of our world has flowed who does not rejoice to be called the king of the Romans. Gallia, however, had grown in such a way in both the fame of its achievements and the excellence of its best men, that it seemed to conquer and surpass the splendor of the rest of the Punic affairs. Now you write to me of its ruin and end. I have no consolation by which I can better alleviate your fortune than by these examples which I also often use, since something has happened to me which is a bit harsh and bitter in my affairs. Nothing, however, is being done in this reign which should be known for its novelty or magnitude; for we are all in such leisure, how much I know not if we have been otherwise, fearing that this might perchance harm virtue itself by all our actions. sample.seedTranslation:
The act of our city in which Gaius Lucius was absolved by the laws and established in that dignity is approved, which he often deserved by fighting most bravely for the fatherland. How much that matter has added to these studies of mine which I undertook for the republic, you will understand shortly; for the glory of our Gaius often excites me from sleep. I shall not rest until I see him equal to those who I judge to be his superiors in age and glory, having followed him in magnitude of mind and magnificently performed deeds. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Not about private conveniences (as often before) but about the safety of our citizens have I signed these letters to you. If there was ever a time that the status of the republic was a care to you, see that on this day you are willing to be present to help them and your son. For a high danger hangs over them, which, unless they are managed by you most attentively, will easily erupt into a great conflagration. Wherefore, again and again, hasten to us. Nor let any matter be so great that it delays your arrival. All who are affected by your presence write that the common safety of all is placed in you alone. Do not, therefore, defer the expectation of all. Persuade yourself that it is better than any principate for a man to be loved by his citizens, and with this glory of all, that he has fled no danger or labor for the republic. You know the benevolence and hope of all the citizens placed in you; write not, you who know everything and love the fatherland greatly, as you will see these things better with yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'F' marks the beginning of the text.</note>The ability, as you wish, to be able to help the republic, certainly I would flee no labor or danger for the common safety. But there are many things that strike me with diffidence and desperation regarding this matter. For many of ours prefer rather to disturb everything, so that they themselves might seem to be in charge, than to live among us with equal law, and there are many in the city who do not understand enough what is in the virtue and liberty of the citizens. If anyone, however, is found in the city who judges and feels well about the republic, his speech is of no value to the multitude. Nor do I see, therefore, what my presence can bring to the fatherland and to our citizens, unless I take upon myself many enmities, which are necessary neither for me nor for the republic. But when it will have come to the opinion that I should commit my safety to these waves and storms of the republic, I will not refuse to try everything for the love of the fatherland, rather than to fail such expectation of our citizens. You have my judgment about the republic. You, as soon as it is decided again about the will of our citizens, hasten to write to me what I am to do. Farewell.

of <term>Caius Cornelius</term> <gloss>a name</gloss>, I follow you. For I have always seen eloquence in the cause of an orator to prevail greatly, to dominate in judgments as if in its own kingdom. But I know not how that matter will be well transacted by me. For in the matter, money is needed, and I, from the previous lawsuit, am exhausted not only in acting (which had been with me), but I am also held by great alien debt. But that I ask and beseech of you, that if you can apply any remedy for some opportunity through others, do not let any occasion pass by. I have decided that I will restore to integrity the hope of my friend, <note>or "my friend who has disappointed my hope"</note>, and that I will not let any patronage be ruined. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>My matter is in safety, and now (as they say) you are sailing into the harbor. For nothing that could be desired by friends was lacking for you for the victory of your cause. For it was fought with study and diligence so that your matter might be brought to where it finally arrived. It was God who was solicitous in this cause of yours as if it were his own, and perhaps even more, because in the cause of friends it is fitting that we be somewhat more attentive than in our own matter. You will say what thanks you owe me and your friends, not because they are ignorant of your mind, but so that your benevolence toward them may be more tenacious. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>It is a bad office which I would call more necessary than that you should be grateful to those by whom we have been well received. Nor was there need for your admonition for me, because all things that are said to you always not only delight me, but I also magnify them. I was writing, therefore, to friends not to pass over that kind of thanks. For after my matter is placed in safety by their study, there is nothing that can be satisfied by me by their office. But I will make it known that I will make no end to living up to this greatest benefit of theirs. To you, truly, I give many thanks who, out of benevolence, have made me more informed than all others about these matters which I most wished to hear. Farewell.

sample.seedTranslation: <note>A red decorative initial 'S' at the beginning of the text.</note>I write to you about religion, which is the one thing that has always been judged by the wisest men to be entirely worthy of our care and our study. For neither would the Roman people have possessed a king, nor would it be called the prince of all nations and peoples, had it not placed religion above every empire and all things. And if they also cultivated what was a false religion for their own truth, I would never judge that their empire could have grown so much, or that it would have stood so long after it grew, had not all their deeds, even the smallest, been initiated first under good auspices and divine worship. What, then, is it fitting for us to judge, for whom the true and immortal religion was first invented by our ancestors, and afterwards published and accepted by us with the best reason? And this is what the Roman people learned, then Sparta and others. Who held the leadership of Greece for a long time. For they thought there was nothing that would better turn men to humanity than if they feared and revered the gods. To act well and faithfully, not a few of our emperors were true followers of the faith if they considered the affairs of peace and war. For those who for a long time referred peace and war to divine worship, all things succeeded prosperously for them, in such a way that, for their victory, often the elements and nature itself fought. Theodosius, by just opinion, is to be numbered among the clear Caesars, since he sought all wars under divine auspices, and bore the name of the one and immortal God inscribed on his standards and banners. He not only had men as aid, but he is read to have had the gods themselves as helpers. Great were the things that were divinely revealed and attributed to Constantine, the first Christian emperor, which, if anyone wishes to consider more attentively, there is no one who does not easily go to the love and study of divine things, not only to be stirred, but also to be vehemently inflamed in mind. When I read this, it is incredible what it stirs up in me about divine things. For I feel my whole mind being renewed, and that I am a far different mind than I was formerly. sample.seedTranslation:
<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> How much I cultivate all my relatives from the heart, you will easily understand if you think about my studies toward them. For everyone's own are dear to each person. But I do not think there is anyone of them whom I know who pursues his own with greater benevolence than I do mine. I cannot sufficiently admire what some men can think of me, whom neither my previous duties toward my own nor my benefits can move, and who go about disparaging me. But words (as I see) are useless to them for other things. They want to be bothersome, and they prefer to speak maliciously rather than benevolently. I have, however, in this sickness and annoyance, one great relief: that we live in a city in which we are both sufficiently known. They will not, however, effect that I should depart from my custom, and so that their eyes may crack more with pain, I will always study to be more dutiful and more kind toward my own. Whatever study can be done by me for you against such men, you will take up the whole of it through our old benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> What great annoyance I received from your letter, because your duties toward all your relatives were sufficiently seen by all the citizens. For I have never been less solicitous for your dignity than for my own. But since there is no one who does not judge most excellently of you, I think it ought rather to be guarded against—their own dignity, by those who desire to lower your good estimation from the minds of men—than that you should have to doubt about your fame. If, however, it happens that you hear otherwise about yourself, I will not bear it dissemblingly, and I will even make it so that those who came prepared to speak maliciously about another will dare much worse things about themselves. Whatever they may plot against you, there is nothing that should greatly disturb you. For the opinion which good men have formed of you is stronger than that it can be violated by such men. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial T.</note> I have cultivated friendship, which is from honesty, above all things, and I have borne nothing else in human affairs with greater regard. Now, however, it would be the most shameful thing to neglect the reason for this, whether of virtue or custom, which I have often placed before many and great things. I will tell you what reason has pushed me to this. For I have so persuaded myself that either there is no good in life, or that it is joined with friendship. If it were done for our own study, I would not admire this good so much. But since I see that all men are led and driven by nature itself to this, that they live together and love themselves, there is no one who does not judge this thing as divine. For not all come to friendship equally; but as each one is worth more in virtue and talent, so he accommodates himself to them more rightly and better. For we see that the studies of men are various: some hope for utility in friends, others for honors; some are excited to those things so that they may have those with whom they may amuse themselves. The wise man, however, places all the fruit of friendship in honesty. And I, when I had decided to love, not through good men, took care not to follow others than those I understood to be pleasing for their own sake. I was afterward so attentive in that matter that I took care of one thing: that I should not be surpassed by any of my own in duty. I will tell you what is true: I love men so that they may be pleased. I never love more than when good things happen to my friends. Even if I do not wish for bad things to happen to them, yet that seems to me the highest time for friendship: either when friends expect our effort more, or when they can love those whom they love from the heart. Those, when there is some sickness of friends, which can be healed by helping, made me besides more dutiful in friendship, because I promised myself that I could not but be loved by them, whom I loved so much, which reason has never deceived me, although I will never be wearied in the love of my own. For I hope that by these reasons I can reconcile the minds of many men to myself. For you yourself have often exhorted me to this matter. I have held your opinion as of such value that I held none more. You will therefore see, according to your wisdom...

<note>A red decorative initial S marks the beginning of the text.</note> I praise and admire your solicitude and the zeal which you used in this matter of mine. I myself, even more so, <note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> will use it for you. It delights me. For I see nothing that can be added to this benevolence of yours toward me. I wish I could give thanks. To return them in deed someday. If you are pleased with this, I would wish it. The memory of your benefits toward me will be everlasting. For as much as I can be moved in my soul, I will accomplish so much that I will think of no thing more often than how I may always do those things which I understand you want and expect. Otherwise, I will assign it to fortune or to my own imprudence if I do not seem to satisfy as much as I ought in your immortal services toward me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> In all business which I know pertains to you, I will give all my labor, care, and zeal. And let this be written by me, that I wish that no gratitude be owed by you to me, which by your merit is already long since given. For you have deserved so well of me that there is nothing that I would hesitate to undertake for you or to accomplish for you. If there is anything in your affair that can be done by me, you will receive it as already done, not in advance. Think that there is no thing so arduous that I would not think it to be very easy, as long as I understand that some duty of mine can be of service to you. See, therefore, that you write to me often about all your affairs, and do not permit me to be idle. For I will think that I am loved by you the most when you have imposed some great thing that is in your interest upon me often. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> That you write to me about your love is customary, and already ancient. For when was there a time in which you did not value my affairs more than your own? For I receive pleasure from the fact whenever I hear something of your benevolence. And I receive no less joy from your letters than if we were commenting in person on these matters of which you write to me. I regret the person who would bring me much pleasure by your presence. at the same time it took away his counsel. They can write to you that everything must be attempted by you. From whom you should depart. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note> In what state I have been, and in what I am placed, I do not think you are ignorant. But that which disturbs me most is that I have neither the spirit nor the counsel by which I can help myself. For I was instituted by nature such that I could not dissimulate my grief, nor was I educated under such precepts that I could patiently bear my poverty. You know how softly I was nurtured by my parents. I could never have hoped to be brought to this indignity, that I should fall from those resources which, earned by great virtue, could have benefited all good citizens. But fortune has deceived my counsels, and it has unexpectedly cast down that most flourishing state of mine in which I long lived happily. For I believed there was at some time an end to these adversities, and (as is said in a trite proverb) that time removes sickness from men. I truly see, however, that I am experiencing what is false. For in the anger of fortune it always recrudesces, and the longer I am in conflict with these discomforts and molestations, the more I feel I am deteriorating. Shame, however, primarily stands in my way. For if I happened to show myself to my friends, or if I confessed my want, much aid would come from them. Such confusion holds my mind that I would rather perish in want than reveal my poverty. You know what it is for a man not ignoble, and who is of a noble spirit, to beg from another. I could scarcely even be induced to give these letters to you, who are most familiar to me. But your faith and benevolence have dispelled all my hesitation. You, for the sake of our friendship, will see again and again if there is anything in which you can help me among our friends. That, indeed, I am prohibited from doing by too much modesty. Farewell.

If, however, a single ecclesiastical or worldly person has done this, he incurs the sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss>, from which no one is absolved unless restitution of the aforesaid has been made, except at the article of death.

¶ The nineteenth principal has two. First, if anyone of those, as above, has come to the Roman curia openly or secretly and has departed from the curia without the license of the lord Pope, he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. Second, if anyone knowingly has received a bishop, as above, lurking near the Apostolic See, or has not taken care to make manifest to the lord Pope or to anyone through whom the notice could be led to him, the reception and arrival of those, he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. These two cases are had in the constitutions of <term>Joh. XXII</term> and <term>Platon. r. c.</term>, <term>Et si doceat</term> <gloss>And if it teaches</gloss>. ¶ The twentieth principal case is confirmed from the Council of Constance by Martin, there in the bull <term>Multo</term> <gloss>Much</gloss>, and in these words: We order them to be suspended by that very fact. Elections, postulations, and confirmations, and whatsoever petitions simoniacally made of churches, monasteries, dignities, personages, offices, and ecclesiastical benefices are null by the law itself, and no right is acquired by them to anyone, nor does the promotion or petition produce its fruits, but those receiving them are held to their restitution as if they were unjustly given; and the givers and receivers incur the sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term>, even if they shine with pontifical or cardinal dignity. ¶ The twenty-first: this is from the Council of Basel 12. Thus, those simoniacally elected or pontiffs or abbots, and those who were the principals of this simoniacal election, and those choosing and confirming, in the horror of such a penalty, incur the sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term>; nor can those elected and confirmed be absolved from such guilt and excommunication unless they freely resign the churches and dignities to which they were shamefully assumed, and they remain perpetually rendered unable to obtain those which they acquired through wicked ingress. ¶ Concerning the cases touching principally religious men and women. ¶ Chapter five.

Here are to be counted the cases that touch religious principally, which are these. The first principal is against religious of the mendicant orders.

sample.seedTranslation: The fifth principal is concerning the immunity of the church and those who, holding temporal dominion by license of anyone, forbid their subjects to sell anything to prelates or clerics or ecclesiastical persons, or to buy anything from the same, or not to grind grain for them, bake bread, or show them other services, is not bound, says the said Pope, except for dukes and prelates. The sixth principal is against those who from churches and ecclesiastical persons, for their own proper goods which they carry or cause to be carried, not for the sake of trading, demand or extort tolls <term>pedagia</term> <gloss>road or bridge tolls</gloss> or suchlike by themselves or others in their name or another, or compel them to pay such, a contrary custom notwithstanding; and the bishop of the place ought to publish them as excommunicated, or cause them to be published by his subjects, until they have restored what was thus exacted and have satisfied for such transgression competently, <term>Extra de censibus</term>, chapter <term>Quaestione</term>, Book 5, § <term>Qui vero</term>, nor do they excuse, says the said Pope, at the time from which memory exists, clerics paying tolls, which the Pope understands of ancient tolls, not of new ones. The seventh principal case contains two. The first: that laymen who formerly through force or fear compelled prelates or the chapter of churches or other ecclesiastical persons to submit to them immovable goods or rights of churches without the consent of the chapter and the license of the Pope, unless they relax such submissions after the requisitioning warning. And that henceforth they compelled prelates or other ecclesiastical persons to do such things. The second: whoever through submission rightly made until now usurps anything beyond that which is permitted by licit tract, unless they desist from such usurpation having been lawfully warned, and restoring also what they have usurped, <term>Extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis</term> <gloss>On not alienating church goods</gloss>, and this in the newest § <term>Laici</term>, Book 6. The eighth principal has two. The first is against those who, under the title of royal custody or guard of their advocacy or defense, attempting to usurp anew in churches, monasteries, or other pious places, presume to usurp the goods of the same churches, monasteries, or pious places that are vacant. The second is against clerics, monks of monasteries, and persons of churches of the same places that allow this to be done, <term>Extra de electione</term>.

sample.seedTranslation: The fourth rule: it is expedient that the confessor obtain for his power from the prelate of his subjects in reserved cases, beyond, or relievers, especially unless there are public and scandalous cases. For very few are found, as the Chancellor <note>Jean Gerson</note> says from there, who have not fallen into some such case that they do not reserve; they indeed, confessors knowing themselves not to be able to be remitted henceforth to another, they detect all things more freely. The confessor indeed presumes to question them more freely and to heal more fully by absolving them once; for what else is it to remit a penitent from judge to judge in hidden things, than to add affliction to the afflicted? Certainly many existing in filth cause more causally or occasionally and become dirtier. Christ did not do so to the Samaritan, of whom Isaiah prophesies thus: he will not crush the bruised reed, and he will not extinguish the smoking flax; he will lead judgment in truth; he will not be sorrowful nor turbulent. ¶ The fifth rule: according to Hubert <note>Hubert of Romans, author of instruction manuals for confessors</note> in his book on the instructions of officials, in the chapter on the hearing of confessions: let him obtain such a place for sitting that he can be seen by many, especially when he hears women, and that the confession cannot be heard by anyone, in which he certainly provides for the fame of both himself and the one confessing. For the confessor is an angel of the Lord of the armies of God, as Malachi says, and concerning the confessor and the one confessing, Christ says: he who does truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested, which were done in God. So also the blessed <term>Jerome</term> informs Nepotian: all suspicions, he says, and whatever can probably be feigned, let it be avoided by you; abstain from all bad appearance, the Apostle commands. ¶ The prelates, however, who submit these rules, easily succumb to suspicion concerning women, says Job: the eye of the adulterer watches for darkness; for, as Hubert says, if some great persons of the male sex wish to confess, of whom the confessor believes that he might be ashamed in the aid of others, he ought to lead them to another place more secret and honest.

Not-obstructing, that is, who has the power to resist without his own danger and does not do it, when he is held by office to obstruct, if in this way thieves grow strong, such as are princes who by their office are held to observe justice because the rents which they have are instituted for this; they are held to make restitution. Otherwise [for those] who are not held by office to observe [justice], because they are not held to restitution.
Not-manifesting, that is, who knows where the robbed or stolen thing is [and] does not indicate it when it is requested, and when he is held to this by office, he is held to restitution; otherwise if he only knows where it is and does not indicate it, even when requested about this, [it is the case] that then one sins, yet he is not held to restitution. Whence a judge who ought to pronounce on the matter of which he knows, and thus manifest the law, if he does not do it, he is held to restitution. From the aforementioned it is also clear that any heir, whether a son or a stranger, without distinguishing the property of the robber or another, is held by canon law to pay all the debts of the deceased, whether they were from contract or quasi-contract, or from a misdeed or another [cause], whether that thing for which the debt was contracted reached him or not, whether the lawsuit was contested with the deceased or not. There is, however, a contract, such as purchase, sale, hiring, letting, loan, and similar; a quasi-contract is such as guardianship or the management of another’s affairs. A misdeed is such as theft, robbery; a quasi-misdeed is when a judge judges through incompetence, or when something is thrown or poured out from another’s house which harmed passers-by.

<note>A red decorative initial O begins the text.</note>Deliver me from my enemies, Lady of the world: arise to meet me, Queen of piety. Adorn yourself in your ornaments: let the sardius and topaz be your diadem. Let the jasper and amethyst be your right hand: let the beryl and chrysolite be your left hand. Let the jacinth and agate be upon your breast: let carbuncles sparkle on your necklaces. Let myrrh, frankincense, and balsam be in your hands: let sapphire and emerald be on your fingers.

<note>A red decorative initial O begins the text.</note>You have turned us away because of our sins: and you have had mercy upon us through the Virgin Mary. Make us joyful with the sweet-flowing sound of your mouth: and pour your rosy nectar into our hearts. Thunder for her from above: and give her praise.

I did not patiently endure the injuries and insults brought upon me. ¶ For the salvation of the souls of friends and enemies, I did not pray to God, and I did not offer the reward of labor to those working for me. ¶ In whatever way I did not fulfill the works of mercy, I state my guilt and render myself culpable to God and to you.

### ¶ On the twelve articles of faith

Seventh, I sinned because I did not firmly believe the twelve articles of faith, nor did I confess them with heart and mouth for righteousness. Indeed, sometimes I doubted concerning them and concerning the sacraments of the altar. I did not have a living and just faith with good works like a good Christian, nor did I defend and preach my faith against Jews, infidels, and heretics. Indeed, I willingly listened to those wandering and arguing against the faith.

### ¶ On the seven sacraments of the Church.

Eighth, I sinned, because I passed over and neglected the seven sacraments of the Church like a good Christian. ¶ First, because although I am baptized, yet I did not renounce the devil and his pomps as I promised in baptism. And although I am confirmed, yet I blushed to speak and preach the faith of Christ and the truth for fear of the world, and I neglected it. I did not honor or keep the order of matrimony. ¶ Ecclesiastical orders

sample.seedTranslation:
fountain of the heart and grace, the true delight of the heart. 
Although I am not able to speak worthily of You, yet I will not be silent; love makes me bold so that I may rejoice concerning You alone. 
Your love, Jesus, is a grateful refreshment of the mind; it fills without satiety, giving desire to the hungry. 
Those who taste You hunger; those who drink still thirst; they cannot desire anything except Jesus, whom they love. 
He whom Your love inebriates knows what Jesus tastes like; the happy taste that satisfies, there is nothing further that he can desire. 
Jesus, angelic beauty, a sweet song in the ear, honey in the mouth, nectar in the heart, heavenly. 
I desire You a thousand times, my Jesus; when will You come to me? When will You make me joyful? When will You satisfy me with Yourself? 
Your continuous love is a persistent longing for me; Jesus, honey-sweet, the perpetual fruit of life. 
Jesus, supreme kindness, wonderful joy of the heart, incomprehensible goodness, Your charity binds me. 
It is good for me to love Jesus, to seek nothing beyond Him, to fail entirely, so that I may be able to live for Him.
